title: Will Canadian workers refuse to handle Israeli goods? Why unions increasingly say they should

blocks.text: Canada·New

A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions. The Canadian Labour Congress, which represents more than 3 million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be “hot cargo," emphasizing a call for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel.
Canadian Labour Congress calls on workers to refuse handling weapons and other goods destined for Israel
A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions and workers are preparing for potential battles with their employers.

The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents more than three million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be "hot cargo" and calling for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. The CLC also resolved to cut ties with the Histadrut, Israel's largest trade union organization.

The moved followed similar resolutions passed by numerous local and provincial labour groups over the past year, including the Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador labour federations.

Next week, the B.C. Federation of Labour will vote on a resolution that would "support affiliate locals and unions in refusing to engage with" Israeli goods and specifically ask the B.C. government to stop importing and selling Israeli wines.
A BCFL spokesperson said in an email that the union does not comment on resolutions before delegates have had a chance to debate them.

The movement to isolate Israel with economic pressure is growing as its deadly strikes on Gaza continue after a ceasefire deal was signed more than a year ago. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, while Israeli officials say five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

blocks.text: "I think the vast majority of union activists have come to see that this is a situation where people of conscience, and workers of conscience, need to do what they can to oppose Israeli crimes and our complicity in them," said Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee that pushed for the resolutions across Canada.

A report by the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory including East Jerusalem and Israel stated last month that Israel has continued to commit genocide since the ceasefire. Israel dismissed the charge as part of a "misinformation campaign."

Israel is facing accusations of genocide before the International Court of Justice, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is wanted on an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.
Union says Palestinian workers made request

Levangie, a member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Atlantic in Halifax, says the Canadian government is not doing enough to stop the flow of weapons to Israel, or the import of products manufactured in illegal settlements in Palestinian territories, so it "falls on Canadian workers" to ensure they are complying with their obligations under international law.

Levangie visited the West Bank as part of a union delegation in September and October, where he met with Palestinian groups, including trade unions, who have asked unions in the West to take on this work.
"We're honouring a request that was made by Palestinian workers," he said.

"In that way, it's very similar to the South African context of the 80s and 90s, where South African trade unions, South African civil society organizations, were asking for us to isolate apartheid South Africa until the freedom struggle was won."
Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee, says workers want to comply with international law. (Submitted by Kevin Levangie)

Canadian dockworkers, postal workers and retail workers joined international campaigns declaring South African goods as hot cargo in the 1980s to pressure the country's government into ending apartheid.

Canadian workers also took hot cargo actions to protest Argentina's human rights abuses and suppression of trade unions in 1979 and joined a trade union boycott of Indonesia in 1999 to protest the country's military occupation of East Timor.

blocks.text: Canadian unions have not acted on the CLC resolution, though workers in other countries have taken action.

Italian workers staged a day-long general strike last month, blocking roads, causing rail delays and cancellations and disrupting airports to protest Israel intercepting an aid flotilla that was carrying food to Gaza.

Canada's unions did not participate in a global day of strike on Oct. 30, which saw efforts to disrupt weapons transfers to Israel as part of a broader anti-war protest at 113 ports across 22 countries.
Critic says Israel singled out
The CLC's resolution has created tension within the labour movement, according to Kim Kazur, labour consultant and adviser with the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee advocacy group.

A retired Ontario Public Service Employees Union member, Kazur says she feels unions are unfairly singling out Israel on the world stage and the resolutions are a way to "hide behind" what she views as "Jew hate."
Kazur says unions should "stay in our lanes" and not contribute to "divisive political ideology," adding workers could end up putting themselves at risk of being fired.

blocks.text: "The idea of a union encouraging its members to do some type of disobedience is not OK," she said.
Levangie denied accusations of hate and noted Labour for Palestine regularly collaborates with advocacy group Independent Jewish Voices in its organizing work.
"We in Labour for Palestine are strongly opposed to antisemitism and all other forms of hate," he said.
Advocates say they want to end Canada's involvement in manufacturing F-35 parts that could end up on Israeli jets. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)
Workers could face discipline

Levangie acknowledges a concern about discipline or retaliation by employers if workers refuse to handle certain goods — from components of F-35 fighter jets that are manufactured in Canada, to oranges shipped from Israel to Canadian grocery stores — but says the declaration of hot cargo is the labour movement's "greatest power."
The tactic is often used in the context of labour disputes, says Andrew Stevens, an associate professor at the University of Regina's school of business.

The BCFL issued a hot cargo edict on Nov. 2 — in solidarity with striking Trigon employees with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 523 — ordering workers not to handle Trigon coal and petroleum products.

blocks.text: Moving to concrete action can be complicated, however, especially on a heated political issue.

"If an individual worker engages in this, I think people are going to see it as insubordination, which means that they could be subject to discipline up to and including termination of employment," Stevens said.
If two or more workers deliberately refuse orders to unload goods or procure services, he says that would be deemed an illegal strike.

Stevens says workers will need strong support from their unions and labour organizations if they plan to carry out the CLC's resolution on the ground.
"Its strength is really going to be premised on the support from the unions themselves," he said.
CBC News has reached out to the CLC for comment but has not heard back.
